metadata.title: Cite & Seek
metadata.topic: Final project pitch: an evaluation-first, citation-grounded code question-answering tool
metadata.purpose: INFO 7375 final project pitch film (2-4 min). Honest about what exists and what will.
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: Show-tell opens with the hesitant writer and has no verdict card. Your Turn and an outro are kept; the outro is our own drawn beat (FILM-PLAN.md).

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Meena. This is my final project for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Prompt Engineering for Generative AI. It's called Cite and Seek.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: 'Introduction' large at top left; 'INFO 7375: Prompt Engineering for Generative AI' types out as the course name is spoken; then 'Final Project' appears.
labels: INFO 7375: Prompt Engineering for Generative AI

beats.narration_text: A tool that answers questions about a codebase with citations to the exact files, and refuses when the code doesn't say.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: A question card enters a dark box labelled 'Cite & Seek'. An answer card comes out carrying the citation tag [app/api/orders.py:52-84]; a second path ends in a slip labelled 'ABSTAIN'.
shot.motion_claim: A question card enters a dark box labelled 'Cite & Seek'. An answer card comes out carrying the citation tag [app/api/orders.py:52-84]; a second path ends in a slip labelled 'ABSTAIN'.
shot.heading: What It Is

beats.narration_text: Three terms. Retrieval: finding the code that matters. A citation: the file and lines behind a claim. Abstaining: refusing when the code doesn't say.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

terms.meaning: the file and lines behind a claim
refuse when the code is silent

beats.narration_text: It runs on a real open-source e-commerce codebase from GitHub, standing in for a company's code, with fifty-three test questions I wrote and checked against the code, plus ten synthetic incident reports.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.motion_claim: A repo crate with three file pages, labelled 'e-commerce API' and 'GitHub · MIT'; a binder labelled '53 questions'; a folder labelled '10 synthetic incidents'.
shot.heading: What It Is

beats.narration_text: My hypothesis is that on a real team, this would help a new engineer understand unfamiliar code without pulling a senior engineer away from their work,

beats.narration_text: It's for someone hiring an entry-level AI engineer. Once it's written up, in their first minute, they will open the README, compare the baseline with each experiment, and check any cited line themselves.

shot.heading: Who It's For
shot.subheading: Target reader: hiring manager for an entry-level AI Engineer role

beats.narration_text: Here's the pipeline that exists today. A question is embedded with Mini-L-M, a small local model, and compared against every chunk of the codebase, each at most two hundred tokens.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: Labelled stages with arrows: question -> MiniLM embed -> search all chunks. Below the search stage, three chunk strips labelled orders.py 52-84, cart.py 27-46, payments.py 1-24, and '≤ 200 tokens'.
shot.motion_claim: Labelled stages with arrows: question -> MiniLM embed -> search all chunks. Below the search stage, three chunk strips labelled orders.py 52-84, cart.py 27-46, payments.py 1-24, and '≤ 200 tokens'.
shot.heading: How It Works

beats.narration_text: The top five chunks go to Claude Haiku four point five, with one rule: use only these chunks, and cite every claim by file and lines.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: Stages with arrows: search -> top 5 (five strips) -> Claude Haiku 4.5 -> answer. The answer carries [app/api/orders.py:52-84]; a rule page reads 'only these chunks · cite every claim'.
shot.motion_claim: Stages with arrows: search -> top 5 (five strips) -> Claude Haiku 4.5 -> answer. The answer carries [app/api/orders.py:52-84]; a rule page reads 'only these chunks · cite every claim'.
labels: only these chunks · cite every claim
shot.heading: How It Works

beats.narration_text: If the chunks don't contain the answer, it replies with a single ABSTAIN line instead of a partial answer.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: From the Claude Haiku 4.5 stage, one arrow reaches a half-written page that is dimmed and labelled 'no partial answers'; the other reaches a slip labelled 'ABSTAIN: what is missing'.
shot.motion_claim: From the Claude Haiku 4.5 stage, one arrow reaches a half-written page that is dimmed and labelled 'no partial answers'; the other reaches a slip labelled 'ABSTAIN: what is missing'.
shot.heading: How It Works

beats.narration_text: So it shows four AI engineering skills: retrieval, citation, abstention, and evaluation. The first three exist in the baseline. Evaluation is what I will build next. In course terms: source grounding, prompt contracts and evaluation.

shot.subheading: In course terms: source grounding, prompt contracts, evaluation

beats.narration_text: What sets it apart is the order: I wrote and checked the test questions before writing any retrieval code, and eight of them have no answer in the code, so refusing will be tested too.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.motion_claim: A locked binder '53 questions' sits before an empty outline 'retrieval code' with an arrow 'first'; eight pages slide out in a row labelled '8 unanswerable'.
shot.heading: Why It's Different

beats.narration_text: The alternative today is reading the code by hand. That's how I checked every answer in my test set. It works, but it's slow, and nothing tells you when you've missed the right file.

shot.motion_claim: A magnifier crawls over five file pages labelled orders.py, cart.py, auth.py, payments.py, models.py; it skips auth.py, which stays dim, labelled 'missed file?'. Label 'by hand'.
shot.heading: Why It's Different
shot.subheading: The alternative: reading the code by hand

beats.narration_text: In scope: one codebase of thirty-seven files, small on purpose, not production scale. Out of scope: agents, fine-tuning, and orchestration frameworks, so every step stays visible.

shot.subheading: In scope and out of scope

beats.narration_text: The first thing I will build is the scoring harness: retrieval hits, and an LLM judge I will check against my own labels. You'll know it ran when its results rebuild with one command.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: Stages with arrows: terminal 'one command' -> 'harness' -> 'results'. Below, a 'judge' row of marks beside a 'my labels' row of dots.
shot.motion_claim: Stages with arrows: terminal 'one command' -> 'harness' -> 'results'. Below, a 'judge' row of marks beside a 'my labels' row of dots.
shot.heading: Scope: In, Out, First

beats.narration_text: The risk is sample size. With an eighty-twenty split, only about six unanswerable questions will be left for tuning, so one refusal will move the rate by about seventeen points. I will report raw counts and confidence intervals.

qc.sparse_reason: Show-tell: one drawn diagram with short labels. Only underfill and clustering waived.

shot.visual_intent: Eight pages split into groups labelled 'about 6' and 'held out'; a gauge needle jumps ('one refusal'), then gets a shaded band labelled 'raw counts'.
shot.motion_claim: Eight pages split into groups labelled 'about 6' and 'held out'; a gauge needle jumps ('one refusal'), then gets a shaded band labelled 'raw counts'.
shot.heading: What Could Sink It

beats.narration_text: Evaluating models on held-out data isn't new to me; retrieval, embeddings, and using one model to judge another are. This project is how I learn them in a way someone else can check.
